# Requirement traceability

Every RFP-020 requirement, what implements it, and what verifies it.

**Generated. Do not edit.** The sources are `traceability/requirements.toml`
(the inventory, transcribed from RFP-020) and `traceability/matrix.toml`
(the mapping). Regenerate with:

```sh
cargo run -p traceability --bin render-traceability
```

`cargo test -p traceability` fails if this file and those sources disagree,
if any evidence below names a test, CI job or document that does not exist,
or if a task id written anywhere in the repository appears in no row. That
check is the deliverable, not the table: an unverified matrix drifts into
fiction by the third milestone.

Statuses are `planned` (nothing implemented yet), `partial` (partly
satisfied, or satisfied by M0 evidence that later tasks extend) and
`verified` (satisfied now, with a test or a CI gate behind it, never a
document alone). M5-06 is the task that has to leave every row `verified`.

Not tracked here: the Servicing obligations from the proposal's *Servicing
and SLA* section. They are contractual rather than code and have no test to
name; monthly operating reports are their evidence.

Right now: **10 verified, 13 partial, 13 planned**, of 36 requirements.

**F1** — Public-mode push aggregator accepting signed RedStone data packages, with the signature path structured so swapping in a future host primitive (precompile or syscall) stays a localised change

Two halves. The verification half landed in M1: the `VerifierBackend` trait (M1-10) is the localised-swap structure, and `InProgramBackend` (M1-11) implements it with the same k256 and tiny-keccak M0 measured. The guest patches in the *mixed* accelerator configuration -- recovery accelerated, keccak in software -- which is M0's recommendation rather than a default. The aggregator half is now standing but empty. M2-01 settled the surface: the instruction set and the feed state in `aggregator-program`, so the host can test them, and the `#[lez_program]` module in `methods/guest/src/bin/aggregator.rs`, because the guest is what LEZ executes -- the shape Logos's own programs use. The guest cross-compiles to riscv32 with SPEL and LEZ linked, which is what proves the surface is buildable rather than only well-formed, and ADR 31 records why the SPEL pin cannot move independently of the LEZ one. The IDL is generated from the guest's own source and `the_committed_idl_matches_the_guest_source` regenerates and compares, so a changed instruction cannot ship an SDK built against a surface the program no longer has. It is a test rather than a CI step because that is what makes the generator addressable from one -- `CARGO_BIN_EXE_generate-idl` reaches a binary and not an example -- and it puts the check on the same `cargo test` a contributor already runs. M2-02 then filled the one instruction that writes a price. `submit_price` reads the clock from the pinned account, decodes the feed it was given, refuses a paused one, verifies through `verifier-core` and publishes -- in that order, so every reachable rejection decidable from the accounts, the stored configuration or the payload's framing lands before the first signature recovery. The rest cannot: an invalid signature and an unmet threshold are what verification exists to answer, and a replayed payload reaches `NotNewer` only afterwards, because that check compares against a timestamp verification has to derive first. The two identifier checks inside `publish` are each after it for a different reason. Its pair check is already done earlier and by someone else, because the pair passed to `verify_feed` is the account's own: a mismatched account answers before `publish` is entered, and by the time it runs its own comparison cannot fail. Its source check is only there, and stays there -- an account derived from the feed and writable only by this program cannot name another source, so hoisting it would buy cycles on a path no caller can reach. The five feeds of the committed capture each go end to end in `a_captured_payload_creates_the_price_account_on_the_first_submission`, on signatures RedStone produced, and the resulting states are handed to LEZ's own `validate_execution` rather than checked against a restatement of its rules. ADR 32 records what the instruction had to decide beyond the verification: one price account per feed at an address derived from the feed's own, created by the first submission that fills it, and open to any caller. The derivation is the part that carries a security property -- without it two feeds registered against the same pair could each write the other's account, which `publish`'s pair check cannot see -- and `a_wrong_price_account_pda_is_refused_by_the_generated_validator` asserts it against the constraint SPEL generates, from the guest workspace, because that code exists only after macro expansion. What is left is the admin half: M2-06 for the gate and M2-07 to M2-10 for registration, signer-set updates, deregistration and pausing. Until M2-07 lands nothing in this repository can register the feed `submit_price` reads, so the push path is exercised and not yet operable.

**F2** — Verification packaged as a library callable both from the aggregator and from third-party consumer programs, so one audited implementation backs both modes

Structural: `verifier-core` depends on neither mode, and both modes depend on it. M3-02 asserts the pull side carries no aggregator dependency. M1-22 supplies the behavioural half: `verifier-core/src/accept_and_reject.rs` reads the accept and reject contract off the crate's public API, which is the surface both modes call. It is tested once rather than once per mode because `verify_feed` takes no argument naming its caller, so there is no per-mode behaviour to reach -- ADR 23 records that, and what the two callers add on top is M2-02 and M3-01, with M3-04 asserting they agree.

**F3** — M-of-N signer threshold per feed, configurable at registration, default 3-of-N; reject any package that does not meet it

`verify_feed` enforces M-of-N over distinct authorised signers: one slot per configured signer, so a signer counts once however many packages it sends (M1-13). A second package from a slotted signer is skipped rather than fatal -- ADR 24 records why, and the tests cover both ways an attacker can produce a duplicate without a key. Which of a signer's packages fills its slot is settled by ADR 27 rather than by ADR 24's freshest rule: the price comes from one round, chosen as the timestamp the most distinct configured signers agree on, and one package files one report however many times it repeats the feed. M1-23 pins the boundaries where an off-by-one would live -- M, M-1, one, and unanimity. ADR 15 records the contract's strict package checks before the threshold is evaluated.

**F4** — Decode the RedStone data-package format (asset identifier, value, timestamp, signer set) and reject any package whose timestamp is older than a configurable `maxAge`, whose value is zero, negative or otherwise invalid, or whose asset identifier does not match the registered feed

Four rejection classes in one requirement. The malformed-wire-format one has landed: M1-12 decodes zero-copy, bounds-checks every length, and is tested against truncation at every offset, since a panic in a guest aborts the transaction rather than rejecting the package. Conformance against published vectors is M1-21. Asset identity has landed (M1-16), and it is a comparison between the caller's expectation and the registration rather than a property of the payload, because a RedStone package names a feed and nothing else -- ADR 16 records what that check does and does not establish. Value sanity has landed too (M1-17): zero, negative and unrepresentable values reject the payload immediately, even when other packages meet the threshold. Staleness has landed as well (M1-14, M1-15): every package for the requested feed must be inside the two-sided window, read from LEZ's pinned every-block clock account. ADR 15 records the strict package-level contract. M1-21 conforms the decoder against payloads captured from RedStone's gateway, using their own signatures as the oracle: a signature recovers to the address they published only if the signed span matches theirs byte for byte, and a negative control shows seven plausible wrong spans recovering nobody. The envelope is covered separately, because it carries no signature and the gateway serves per-signer JSON rather than a finished payload: `sample-data/payload.hex` from the Rust SDK is vendored, and `an_envelope_redstone_published_decodes_and_every_package_in_it_recovers` asserts it decodes and that all fifteen packages recover. The EVM connector is BUSL and is not read. ADR 19 records why the two sources answer different questions.

**F5** — Publish the verified price into a canonical RFP-019 price account, populating base and quote asset, price, timestamp, source identifier (a constant identifying RedStone) and a zero confidence interval (RedStone publishes none)

The account is RFP-019's, re-exported rather than forked (M1-09), and `publish` decides what goes in its six fields. `source_id` is the constant F5 names: `RedStone`, ASCII right-padded, so a consumer checking where a price came from needs nothing from this repository to construct it. ADR 22 records the decision, including why the writer's own identity was the wrong answer: `source_id` is one of the three identifiers `publish` refuses to overwrite, so an identifier that moved with the program id would leave a rebuilt adaptor unable to update the accounts it created. The pair comes from the registration claim (M1-16), the price is the median on the account's Q64.64 scale (M1-17), the timestamp is the observation's and not the write's, and the confidence interval is zero because RedStone publishes none. M1-26 conforms the layout in both directions. M2-02 supplied the caller: `submit_price` writes the account inside a transaction, and `a_captured_payload_creates_the_price_account_on_the_first_submission` asserts all six fields against packages RedStone signed -- the pair from the registration, the median on the account's scale from the capture's own decoded values, the round's timestamp, the `RedStone` constant and a zero interval. `an_update_moves_price_and_timestamp_and_nothing_else` is the other half: the four identifiers survive an update, and so do the owner, balance and nonce that are the account rather than its contents. What is still open is what a consumer does with it, which is M2-04's read path.

**F6** — Admin authority (RFP-001 via SPEL) can register feeds, update a feed's signer set on roster changes, and deregister feeds

The authority has landed and all five operations it guards. `register_feed` is M2-07: a feed lives at the address its id derives (ADR 33), so a client finds one without being told where it is and one feed id has one account. Its parameters are refused by `FeedConfig::try_new` rather than by a second set of rules, so a registration and a submission agree about what a usable feed is by construction. `update_signer_set` is M2-08: the set and the threshold move together, and a rotation names its feed as well as addressing it so the wrong account cannot be handed. `deregister_feed` is M2-09, and it is where ADR 33's address decision had to be paid for: LEZ forbids handing an account back, so retirement empties the data and keeps the account, and `register_feed` grew a third pre-state so a feed id is not spent the first time it is retired. A retirement leaves the *price* account alone, though, and `submit_price` reads the expected pair from it on every write but the first -- so `register_feed` also reads it and refuses a re-registration that would change the pair (`PairChanged`), which would otherwise produce a feed whose every submission answers `AssetMismatch`. `pause_feed` and `unpause_feed` are M2-10, and pausing is the one lever that does not change what a price means -- the set, threshold, window and pair are untouched, so resuming restores exactly the feed that was paused. `submit_price` enforces it before any cryptography. All five operations are now behind the gate and every one names its feed as well as addressing it, so no administrative instruction can reach an account `register_feed` did not claim. All five also answer `FeedDeregistered` rather than `FeedUndecodable` on a retired feed, which is the state a retirement leaves and not a damaged account -- one state, one answer, whichever instruction meets it. `[M2-06:01]` records what M1-07 could not settle: RFP-001's library is written but unmerged, and the surface it needs is larger than the check M2-06 was scoped as -- an authority has to be stored somewhere, and none of the six instructions M2-01 declared could establish one. So it is an account this program owns, at an address the constraint publishes rather than the program explains, and `authorise` is what the administrative instructions call; each takes that account beside the signer. The bodies are M2-07 to M2-10 and all of them have landed. Establishing it is gated on a genesis key the build carries rather than on being first, because a PDA hashes the program id and the program id is the image id: a build that moves the image id presents a fresh default config account, so an unguarded first write is a race once per build whose winner sets the signer sets that decide what a price means. Not once per deployment -- a rebuild from unchanged inputs reproduces the id and lands on the config account it already established, measured in `[M2-06:01]`. A handover is two steps, nominate then accept, because a one-step transfer makes any mistyped key the authority immediately and that state is terminal -- every administrative instruction stops, `initialise` refuses a config account that is no longer default, and rebuilding to recover strands the accounts the build created. The nominee's own signature is what a key nobody controls can never produce. Revocation is exposed because F6 names RFP-001's authority and revocation is one of its hard requirements, and it clears any pending nomination so a nominee cannot accept an authority its holder gave up; what it costs a serviced feed is in the ADR. The check is Rust here and not `#[require_admin]`, because a gate injected into macro-expanded dispatcher code has no reachable host test -- the four admin tests in the guest workspace, six in all, are the shape that forces -- and SEC2 asks for the unauthorised-caller reject to be tested rather than asserted. `tests/admin.rs` is the other half of that: the post-states go to LEZ's own `validate_execution`, and the claim is checked against the address the constraint derives rather than against a restatement of the rule. Its signer fixture is an account some program owns -- owned, funded, having signed before -- because a fixture built from `Account::default()` would pass every assertion while describing a state no real key is in after its first transaction. Ownership is the property and not existence, so `initialise` and `accept` refuse a default-owned key outright (`AdminUnowned`): LEZ strands such an account after one transaction, and on `accept` the authority has already moved by then: LEZ bumps every signer's nonce outside program execution, and rule 7 refuses a post-state whose owner is the default one unless the pre-state was pristine. `an_unowned_admin_that_has_transacted_cannot_be_used` pins both directions, so the deployment property the ADR states -- the admin key is an existing account and not a fresh address -- is asserted here rather than assumed.

**F7** — BTC/USD, ETH/USD, SOL/USD, XMR/USD and ZEC/USD registered on LEZ devnet/testnet as part of the deliverable

M2-00 confirmed all five feeds are published on `redstone-primary-prod`, including the two privacy assets that could not be assumed, and `FEEDS.md` records what it found. One roster of five signers covers all five feeds, every address recovered from the package signature rather than read off the gateway's label, because the roster is what a feed is registered with. Sharing a roster turned out to be a property of the data service and not of these five: a sweep of all 878 feeds it serves found one roster and no exception. The set is the observed one and not an authorised one -- a signer authorised upstream but silent through the sample would not appear -- so M2-08 remains the path for what the observation missed. Rounds land every ten seconds nominally, but three of twenty-six intervals in the sample were double that and an earlier sample held one of thirty seconds, so what a staleness floor has to clear is the worst gap and five minutes only bounds it from below. ADR 30 records why the identical rosters are still stored per feed. M2-11 and M2-12 then registered all five on a chain and published a price for each: `the_push_path_verifies_and_publishes_across_a_real_sequencer` loops F7's five ids through registration and submission against a standalone sequencer, reads each price account back, and then -- after all five have published -- re-reads all five from the chain and asserts they are five distinct accounts each still holding its own feed's price. That is per-feed *account* isolation, where the addresses are the chain's rather than a host fixture's, and deliberately not R3: R3 is about an upstream error for one feed leaving pushes for the others alone, and this loop introduces no upstream failure at all. An earlier version of this note claimed R3's name for it. Five signers registered and three signing, the shape `FEEDS.md` observed and RFP-020 defaults to: two registered signers stay silent on every submission, so the threshold is the binding constraint and the published price is a median over a genuine subset rather than over the whole roster. One deviation, and it is forced rather than chosen: the five are registered with the test's own signing keys, not RedStone's. A live chain reads the clock in real time, `MAX_MAX_AGE_MS` caps a feed at fifteen minutes, and the committed captures are weeks old, so RedStone's signatures cannot be submitted to a running sequencer under any `maxAge` a feed may legally register. Their real signatures are verified by M1-21's conformance suite instead, against those captures, with their published addresses. The combination neither covers is real signatures on a live chain, which needs live gateway data at submit time and belongs to the relayer (M4) and testnet (M5). So the row stays partial for the reason the requirement names rather than for lack of evidence: F7 says devnet or testnet, and a standalone sequencer is neither. The same applies to the task, which an earlier version of this note got wrong: **M2-12 is closed** by the above -- "exercise all five feeds end to end" is what it asks and what happened -- but **M2-11 is not**, because it says register on devnet and this registered on a standalone sequencer. M2-11 stays open, with the harness work done and only the network missing, and S1 is where the network lands, in M5-01 and M5-02.

**F8** — Relayer as a Logos module with a Logos Core headless daemon: configurable data service and feeds, heartbeat and deviation triggers, parallel gateways with first-success, retry and back-off, structured logging, wallet-balance monitoring, clean shutdown

Equilibrium operates this under the SLA, so its logging, wallet monitoring and shutdown paths are deliverables rather than conveniences.

**F9** — Public-mode pull verification library: given a payload, a configured (dataServiceId, feedId, authorised signer set, M-of-N threshold, maxAge) and the consumer's expected (base_asset, quote_asset), returns the verified price and timestamp or a typed error, with no dependency on the aggregator's price account

M3-01 is the surface: one function over `verifier-core`'s own types, returning a verified price or a typed reason. The only type it adds is `PullConfig`, two public fields over a `FeedConfig`, so there is still one validated configuration shape behind both modes. That thinness is what makes the independence this row is about structural rather than reviewed -- there is no aggregator type in the signature and no path that could reach one. `a_consumers_own_configuration_verifies_a_captured_payload` runs all five captured feeds through it with a consumer-supplied signer set, threshold and window, and no feed registered anywhere, asserting that every captured signer reported rather than that the threshold was met -- the second cannot fail, since a verification below the threshold is an error. `a_package_the_consumer_did_not_authorise_is_refused_outright` is the other half of the signer set being the consumer's, and it is named for what it asserts: an unauthorised package aborts the verification rather than going uncounted, so it is not an M-of-N case. The threshold itself is `verifier-core`'s, which takes no argument naming its caller and so has no per-mode behaviour for either mode's suite to reach (ADR 23). [M3-01:01] covers the one place the crate takes a position rather than delegating: the clock is the account and not a parameter, refused unless it is the pinned every-block one. It also records what that does not establish, which matters for this row. The id and the data arrive as two slices, so nothing here can check that the bytes came from the account they name -- binding them needs the `AccountWithMetadata` a dispatcher hands a program, and that type is in a `std` crate a `no_std` library cannot take. The push path has no such residual, because there the two are fields of one chain-supplied struct. So the account-side half is the consumer's, and M3-06 has now discharged it: `settle` in `reference-consumers/pull` takes the clock as one `AccountWithMetadata` and reads its id and its bytes out of that struct, so the two cannot disagree because neither is constructed. `a_clock_account_the_caller_chose_cannot_fill_an_order` covers the mistake that remains reachable -- the 10- and 50-block accounts, which hold real timestamps and are therefore the plausible error rather than an obvious one. Replacing that read with the pinned constant fails it and `no_refusal_returns_a_post_state`, which is what makes the binding load-bearing rather than a matter of style. `PullConfig` is the tuple this requirement names, so the `dataServiceId` is carried -- and `the_data_service_label_changes_nothing_about_a_verification` is what keeps it honest, requiring the same payload and roster to verify identically under any label. It cannot be checked: a payload names no data service, and the one envelope slot that could carry one sits outside every signature, so the signer set is the binding and the label is the consumer’s own record of where its roster came from. It stays off the aggregator stored feed, which the proposal specifies as `(asset id, M-of-N, authorized signer set)`. The `no-std` job keeps the crate linkable by a consumer that does without `std`, which is the other half of being usable inline. M3-02 is the independence half, and it is a gate rather than a test on purpose: no test can observe a dependency that is absent, and the way this requirement would be lost is an addition that compiles and passes everything above. So `pull-independence` pins the resolved build closure of `pull-lib`, of `reference-consumers/pull` and of the consumer's guest workspace to an allow-list -- `verifier-core` and `kanon-clock`, nothing aggregator-side, and an allow-list rather than a denylist because a denylist only refuses the reuse someone thought of. Everything in the closure that does not come from a registry is listed, this repository's own crates and anything reached by path or by git alike -- which it has to be, because the canonical price account is declared in `twap_oracle_core` and arrives by git, so a list of local crates would have left the aggregator's own account type reachable. Registry packages are `cargo deny`'s business. The walk covers every feature and every target rather than the runner's defaults, both of which would otherwise leave a way past: an optional dependency reached through a feature nobody enables, and a dependency declared for the riscv32 guest this crate actually ships into. Dev-dependencies are outside it, which is what leaves M3-04 free to compare the two paths against each other in a test. M3-03 and M3-04 add the signer-set and typed-error halves. M3-06 adds the third walk, and it is the one this requirement is really about: the artefact somebody copies is the program, not the library, and a program is a guest binary. `[M3-06:01]` records why that meant a separate guest workspace -- `cargo tree` resolves a package rather than a binary, and the package holding the aggregator's guest depends on `aggregator-program` and `kanon-idl`, so a consumer built there would sit in a closure containing the push aggregator with no walk able to say it did not use it. The consumer's closure adds LEZ and SPEL and stops there, which holds because `twap_oracle_core` reaches this repository through `kanon-idl` and through nothing else: a program can take the account types it cannot do without and still have no path to the account the push mode writes. Both directions were run -- injecting `aggregator-program` into the guest manifest brings `kanon-idl` and `twap_oracle_core` with it and fails the diff. The sequencer was what was left, and M3-07 has supplied it. A consumer verifying a real payload with nothing registered *against the aggregator* was already asserted over the committed capture and against SPEL's generated validator; `the_pull_path_verifies_and_settles_across_a_real_sequencer` is the same claim through a running LEZ, settling an order from a payload the consumer verifies itself. What holds the independence is the closure walk, which is gated: `ci:pull-independence` walks `pull-lib`, the pull consumer and its guest workspace and fails if an aggregator crate appears. The sequencer suite deploys no aggregator and reads no price account, which shows the pull path does not *need* what the walk proves it cannot reach -- but that suite lives in `e2e`, which the walk does not cover and where `aggregator-program` is a dev-dependency, so its silence is a convention held by the file's own header rather than a gate. The qualification is load-bearing rather than pedantic: the reference consumer does register feeds, with its own authority, in accounts it owns, and a settlement will not verify until it has. What F9 refuses is a dependency on the push mode's price account, which is what the closure walk reads; `[M3-06:02]` records why holding a roster in the consumer's own account is not the thing this requirement forbids. One thing this row deliberately does not cover, so that its scope is not read wider than it is: where a consumer gets the payload in the first place. F9 is the library and the program that verify bytes already in hand, and the fetch is somebody else's -- the relayer's DDL fetch over HTTPS is M4-02 under F8, and what a consumer integrating pull should be told about doing it itself belongs to S4's README and S5's doc packet, both still planned. That documentation owes a reader one thing this repository has not written down anywhere: a pull consumer that fetches from RedStone's gateway at read time exposes the fetcher's address to RedStone, which on a privacy-first chain is a consideration rather than a footnote, and it is the reason the alternative -- taking the bytes from a relayer, or from the transaction itself -- is worth spelling out beside the pattern. `reference-consumers/pull/src/lib.rs` names the trade where a consumer author will meet it; the recommendation is S5's.

**U1** — SDK for building Logos modules in both modes, exposing helpers ergonomic enough that switching modes leaves payload handling unchanged

The mode-switch ergonomics are the testable part: the same payload handling has to serve both paths.

**U2** — Basecamp mini-app dashboard: live prices, signer set, threshold, latest timestamp and staleness per feed, plus a public-mode pull dry-run panel

Built from the M4-18 designs rather than ahead of them; M4-20 is the pull dry-run panel, M4-21 the Basecamp load and flow tests.

**U3** — CLI covering both modes: submit, query the canonical account, register and deregister feeds, update signer sets, and an off-chain pull dry-run reporting the same typed errors as the on-chain library

The dry-run has to report the same typed error codes the on-chain pull library returns, which is what ties M4-16 to M3-04.

**U4** — IDL for the adaptor program and the RFP-019 price-account standard, re-exported rather than forked, via SPEL

Two IDLs, and only one of them is this repository's to define. The price account's stays RFP-019's: re-exported, not forked, with `reference/twap_oracle-idl.json` vendored at a named commit so the conformance test can notice the two disagreeing. The adaptor's own is M2-01's, at `kanon-idl/aggregator-idl.json`, and it is generated from the guest program's source rather than written, so it cannot describe a surface the program does not have. Five entries hold it, because the surface is declared twice and SPEL joins the halves positionally: `spel-cli` encodes an instruction's discriminant as its index in the IDL while the guest decodes it as the declaration index of `Instruction`, so two variants of the same shape could be swapped in one place only and a caller's deregistration would arrive as a pause. The parity tests assert the discriminant and the per-variant argument order against `risc0_zkvm::serde`, which is the codec the transaction actually uses. Reference consumer B now carries the same three parity tests and its own regeneration check, so four of the five names above resolve in more than one crate: `the_committed_idl_matches_the_guest_source` in three, the three parity tests in two each, and only `the_vendored_idl_declares_the_fields_we_expect` in one. The two programs declare their surfaces the same way, so they are held to it the same way, against one implementation of the check that both include by path. One limit of that worth stating rather than leaving to be discovered: `every_piece_of_evidence_resolves` matches a `test:` name by searching every Rust source for the function, with no crate qualifier, so a name cited here is satisfied by any crate declaring it. For the four above that means this row would still read as evidenced if the aggregator's copy were deleted and the consumer's left standing. The citations are accurate today and the gate is weaker than they look; scoping a citation to a crate is a change to the matrix format rather than to this row. The consumer earned them by moving its instruction enum out of `#[lez_program]` and into its library, which M3-07 needs and which took the ordering out of the macro's hands -- `[M3-06:01]` records that. What is left for M4-12 is publishing the artefact as a standalone deliverable and generating the CLI from it.

**U5** — SPEL enhanced so a new program can hook in pull and push feed modes easily

A change to SPEL, exercised from a fresh scaffold program so the hook is shown to work outside this repository.

**U6** — Clear, actionable errors for every failure mode: stale package, threshold not met, unauthorised signer, asset mismatch, malformed package, invalid signature, zero or negative price

One error enum in `verifier-core` is what makes push and pull report the same failure the same way; M3-04 asserts the parity. M1-18 defines the payload and configuration failures, while later hardening added `TooManyPackages` and `TimestampMismatch`. ADR 15 requires strict package rejection: `InvalidSignature`, `UnauthorisedSigner`, `StalePackage`, `FuturePackage`, `ValueOutOfRange` and `TimestampMismatch` return immediately for any package carrying the requested feed, before threshold evaluation. Every public variant has a producer. Duplicate packages cannot fill another signer slot and ADR 24 keeps them non-fatal, so they are not represented as an unreachable error. M1-22 provides the contract-shaped suite and asserts that no two causes collapse onto the same variant. M3-01 puts the second caller behind that enum: `pull-lib` returns `VerifyError` unchanged rather than wrapping it, so the parity M3-04 asserts is an identity and not two taxonomies kept in step. `pull-lib/tests/pull.rs` reads the shared cases back through the pull path, which is what makes the claim about both modes rather than about the crate the enum lives in. M3-04 asserts the identity itself, over the same inputs put to both callers: `every_shared_cause_is_the_same_value_in_both_modes` covers a malformed payload, an unauthorised signer, a threshold the payload cannot reach, a stale package and one dated past the allowed skew, and `an_asset_mismatch_is_the_same_refusal_from_two_carriers` covers the sixth, separately because the pair a caller claims is account state in push and an argument in pull. What is measured in both modes is those six; `InvalidSignature`, `ValueOutOfRange`, `ScalingOutOfRange`, `TimestampMismatch` and `TooManyPackages` need a crafted payload that only `verifier-core`'s `cfg(test)` builder produces (ADR 21), so for those the identity rests on `verify_feed` taking no argument naming its caller (ADR 23) and on `pull-lib` returning the error unchanged -- structural rather than measured, which is worth stating rather than implying every mode was compared. Four asymmetries are named, and two of them asserted rather than described: the clock is `SubmitError::Clock` in push and `VerifyError::NoClock` in pull, one leaf cause under two wrappers routed through the same `clock_code`; a configuration failure reaches push when it decodes a stored feed and reached a pull consumer earlier, at `FeedConfig::try_new`; the claimed pair arrives by different carriers; and the account layer is push's alone. The clock has `a_clock_failure_is_one_cause_under_two_wrappers`, which pins the two leaf values, the difference in wrapper and the number they share; the carrier has `an_asset_mismatch_is_the_same_refusal_from_two_carriers`. The configuration moment has no test, and the account layer has only `every_submit_cause_is_classified`, whose value is the wildcard-free match forcing the next `SubmitError` variant to be classified rather than its assertions, which restate the match above them. That gate matters because the push taxonomy grew four times during M3. `[M3-04:01]` records why the test lives in `aggregator-program` with `pull-lib` as a dev-dependency: a dev-dependency sits outside `--edges normal,build`, so it cannot enter `pull-lib`'s closure. The `pull-independence` job is what refuses the reverse, and it has been run against this edge: both closures still come back as the allow-list with this dependency in place. The two reasons are recorded separately because a reader who takes the second for the first will look to CI for a guarantee that is cargo's.

**U7** — Two reference consumer programs, one per mode, each showing asset-pair verification, staleness handling, typed-error handling and refuse-on-unavailable

Two consumers, one per mode, and both have landed. Refuse-on-unavailable is the pattern being demonstrated: a consumer must never fall back to an unsafe default. They hold the same limit order on purpose, so the two differ in one thing -- where a price comes from -- and a reader can put them side by side. M3-06 is a limit order in the smallest program that can hold one and still govern what it trusts -- `open_order` records a price somebody will trade at, `settle` fills it if a payload the program verifies itself says the market reached it -- and the domain is thin so that what a reader takes from it is the seam rather than the trade. Two of its eight instructions are that domain; the other six are the authority and the per-feed trust accounts the roster lives in, which is the ratio the requirement actually implies: the verification call is one line, and everything around it is what makes the roster the consumer's rather than its caller's. All four things the requirement names are there. Asset-pair verification is worth stating in full, because the obvious way to satisfy the words does not satisfy the requirement: passing the trust account's own pair as `verify_feed`'s expected one holds a value against itself, so `AssetMismatch` is unreachable and nothing is being verified. Nothing on the wire says which assets a feed prices -- no signer attests to it -- so a registration labelling RedStone's `BTC` feed as ETH/USD verifies real BTC packages, meets the threshold, passes every freshness check, and fills an order whose owner believed it was trading ether. The owner's own expectation is the only thing that can catch it, so `open_order` takes the pair the owner is signing for, refuses the order if the registration disagrees (`a_mislabelled_registration_cannot_fill_an_order_its_owner_did_not_intend`), and stores it; a settlement compares that against the registration. `an_order_cannot_be_filled_under_a_pair_its_owner_never_signed_for` is what makes it a live check rather than a described one, and it is reachable because a registration is retirable: the authority may retire a feed and register the id again under another pair, and an order opened before that must not fill under the new meaning. Passing the trust account's pair instead fails that test and no other. Staleness is `FeedTrust::max_age_ms`, what the authority registered for the feed and not something a payload or its sender can widen, with both edges covered: `a_payload_past_the_registered_window_cannot_fill_an_order` asserts the far edge is inside the window and one millisecond past it is `StalePackage`, and `a_payload_dated_past_the_clock_cannot_fill_an_order` is the other side, a different cause because an operator chasing a clock skew needs to be told which. Typed-error handling is `SettleError`, one number per leaf cause with no wildcard arm over `VerifyError`, so a variant added upstream stops the consumer compiling until somebody decides what to tell its callers; `no_two_causes_answer_with_the_same_number` covers every leaf including the configuration and verification blocks, and `the_number_a_caller_sees_is_the_frameworks_offset_one` pins the value a caller actually reads. Refuse-on-unavailable is `no_refusal_returns_a_post_state`, and it is named for what would break it rather than for what it checks: a consumer that answered a failed verification with `Ok` and an unchanged account would leave a caller unable to tell 'the market has not reached your limit' from 'nobody could verify a price', and a caller that cannot tell those apart retries the wrong one. Six real causes are put through it, and each is an error rather than a quiet no-op. One of them is a roster the authority narrowed, which is the case a consumer with a compiled configuration could not have. The numbers are this consumer's own and are deliberately not the aggregator's -- `[M3-06:02]` records why an integer space is per program while the typed value is shared, which is the identity U6's row is about. M3-05 is the other consumer, and it holds the same limit order so the two crates differ in one thing and can be read side by side: where B verifies a payload, this one reads the account the push mode wrote. Which account is the question the mode turns on, and it was never M2-04's -- that row is about the price account not being writable by consumers, and a read in push mode is an account read that sends this adaptor no transaction. Nothing in the six published fields says who wrote one: `source_id` is the constant `RedStone` on every Kanon feed, so it names the data's origin rather than a program. The only binding is the address, which hashes the aggregator's program id, which is its image id -- so `read_price` derives that address from the feed's registration and refuses any other account before it reads a field. `a_price_account_the_caller_chose_cannot_fill_an_order` and `an_account_that_is_not_this_feeds_price_account_is_refused_first` are the two halves of that, and the owner is checked as well as the address because an address is not a guarantee about who filled it: `an_account_squatting_the_address_is_not_the_aggregators` covers the third state. All four things the requirement names are here too, and each answers differently from B's. The pair is three records and two comparisons -- the account's is the aggregator's claim, the source account's is this consumer's authority's, the order's is its owner's -- so `a_price_account_pricing_another_pair_is_refused` and `an_order_cannot_be_filled_under_a_pair_its_owner_never_signed_for` are both live, and removing either fails only its own test. Staleness is the consumer's own window rather than the aggregator's, because a published price starts ageing when it is written: `one_millisecond_past_the_window_is_stale` holds the far edge and `a_price_dated_further_ahead_than_skew_explains_is_refused` the near one, a different cause because an operator chasing a clock skew needs to be told which direction it is out. Typed errors are `ReadError` and `SettleError` with no wildcard arm, and `no_two_causes_answer_with_the_same_number` counts every leaf across all six blocks rather than per module, since a collision between blocks is the one a per-module test cannot see. Refuse-on-unavailable is `no_refusal_returns_a_post_state`, and `a_feed_nothing_has_been_published_for_cannot_fill_an_order` is the case the name is about: a registered feed before its first submission is a pristine account, and answering that with a zero price rather than an error is exactly the unsafe default U7 forbids. `an_order_survives_the_aggregator_being_rebuilt` is the one that makes the arrangement more than plumbing, and `[M3-05:01]` records why: a compiled aggregator id fails safely -- the address goes dead and every read refuses -- and recovers badly, because following the rebuild means rebuilding the consumer, which moves the consumer's own accounts and abandons every open order. The sequencer was what remained, and M3-07 has run reference consumer B against a standalone one: it establishes an authority, registers a roster, opens an order and settles it against a payload it verifies itself, all on chain. The second half is what a compiled roster could not have done -- the authority rotates to a disjoint signer set and an order opened afterwards settles against a payload only the new signers signed, which is `[M3-06:02]`'s decision working rather than described.

**R1** — A price read is read-only and never modifies adaptor state

In push mode a read is an account read: a consumer decodes the canonical `OraclePriceAccount` and sends this program no transaction at all, so there is no read instruction to make read-only and none to test. The requirement is therefore asserted from the other side, on the surface a caller actually sees -- of the ten instructions the IDL declares, exactly one takes a price account it may write, and it is `submit_price`. `only_a_submission_may_write_a_price` pins that against the committed artefact. `register_feed` is why it is a test rather than a glance: it does take the price account, because it reads the pair a feed id has already published so a re-registration cannot repoint the id at another pair (ADR 33), and it takes it read-only and returns it untouched -- `the_post_states_are_the_feed_then_the_three_it_passes_through` asserts the post-state equals the pre-state. An instruction that acquired a *writable* price account merely to read it would pass every test that checks what a body returns, since a post-state equal to its pre-state satisfies them all; the IDL is where that becomes visible. `an_update_moves_price_and_timestamp_and_nothing_else` covers the converse for the one writer: the instruction that may write moves only the two fields a new observation changes. The pull side writes nothing by construction -- `verify_price` takes slices and returns a value -- and M3-01 carries it. M3-05 is the same claim from the consumer's side, which is where it is falsifiable rather than merely true: reference consumer A really does read a price account, and `this_program_never_asks_to_write_a_price_account` reads off its own published IDL that the account it reads is not writable, while `a_settlement_returns_one_post_state_per_account_it_was_given` asserts the account comes back from a settlement exactly as it was handed over. It could not write one in any case -- the account belongs to the aggregator and LEZ refuses a data change by a program that does not own it -- so what these pin is that the consumer never asks, which is the part a caller building a transaction can see.

**R2** — Feed registration is atomic: partial failure leaves existing registrations intact

Atomicity is structural rather than engineered: LEZ applies a state diff whole, so a body that returns `Err` writes nothing at all and no registration can fail after writing part of itself. That is what R2 asks for and it holds for every instruction in this program, not only this one. Uniqueness is a separate property the address decision buys -- a feed lives at the address its id derives (ADR 33), so a second registration of one id is refused before anything is written and two ids cannot collide -- and it is why `register_feed` needs no rollback path. Both are asserted below; the atomicity reading is the one a reader checking the requirement should find first. What neither covers is a squatted address: the account can be made permanently unwritable by anyone, which is a platform question rather than this program's, recorded in `m0/versions.md` question 4 and pinned at both layers by `a_derived_address_can_be_squatted_and_this_pins_the_refusal` and `a_squatted_feed_account_passes_the_validator_and_the_body_refuses_it` -- the second recording which layer answers. The feed account carried `#[account(init)]` until M2-09 needed a third pre-state for it; the dispatcher answered `AccountAlreadyInitialized` then, and the body's `AlreadyRegistered` answers now. Permanent either way.

**R3** — An upstream error on one feed does not affect push mode for other feeds handled by the same node

Isolation here is structural, and saying so is the honest version: `submit_price` is a pure function over the accounts it is handed, so two feeds share no state a test could corrupt from one side and observe from the other. What they could share is an *address*, and that is what the evidence is about. A submission takes three accounts -- the feed, its price account and the clock -- and the only writable one is that feed's own price account, which `only_a_submission_may_write_a_price` reads off the IDL. `a_submission_writes_only_its_own_feeds_price_account` holds each feed at the address its own id derives, asserts the two price accounts differ, and then has BTC publish and ETH publish and each get its own price; a derivation that ignored the feed id fails it, which was checked by making one. `two_feeds_are_two_accounts` pins the feed-account half and `rotating_one_feed_leaves_another_alone` the administrative one. `every_upstream_failure_refuses_with_its_own_cause_and_writes_nothing` covers the failures a payload can carry -- malformed, a roster authorising none of its signers, one the clock has left behind -- asserting the exact cause per case rather than that something failed, because an earlier version answered `Config(DuplicateSigner)` while claiming to exercise `UnauthorisedSigner`. That a refusal writes nothing at all is R2's atomicity and is the return type rather than a test: a body that refuses yields `Err` and not post-states, so nothing partial survives for another feed to inherit. What this row does not reach is the relayer: R3 names "the same node", and a node that stops submitting for every feed because one upstream is down is a failure this program cannot see. That is the relayer's isolation and it is M4's.

**R4** — Temporary upstream errors leave the daemon recoverable, able to push again once feeds return

Fault injection and restart, not just a retry loop: the requirement is about the state the daemon is left in.

**P1** — A single 3-of-N verify-and-publish completes within one LEZ public transaction at the budget in force at delivery, in both modes

M0 measured a 3-of-N update at 1,906,737 cycles against LEZ's 32M per-transaction budget, 5.68%, and pinned it with a guardrail test. That is the typical case; the ceiling is the other half, because the package count sits in the payload's envelope and a hash plus recovery costs about 602,700 cycles per package. Unbounded, 56 of them overran the budget and the transaction aborted instead of publishing. ADR 25 bounds it and `the_most_a_payload_can_cost_still_fits_in_one_transaction` asserts the bound holds. That covers verification and not the read: LEZ reads a program's whole instruction data before the program's first instruction, at about 113 cycles a byte, so a 127,814-byte payload overran the budget on the read alone with verification still correctly bounded. ADR 26 sets `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` at 32 KiB and the largest payload the decoder accepts reads and verifies in 23,042,390 cycles, 69% of the budget. Between the two this row is now a statement about every payload rather than about the captured one. Bounding `InstructionData` itself is LEZ's, not this adaptor's -- no program can refuse bytes it has already been charged for -- so the limit is also a number for the relayer and the aggregator to enforce before submitting. M2-02 supplied the push instruction, and it is one instruction: `submit_price` verifies and writes in a single call, with the payload as instruction data and no chained call to anything. M2-19 is now the evidence that this holds on a chain rather than only in the type: one `SubmitPrice` transaction, carrying the payload as its instruction data, verifies and publishes across a standalone sequencer, and an update at a later round does the same -- so "single transaction" is a statement about executed transactions and not about the shape of the code. M2-18 supplies the price of it, and the answer is that the write is not where the money goes: 7,386 cycles for a first write and 8,582 for an update, against 3,039,832 to verify the same payload -- under three tenths of one percent of the `submit_price` body either way, and 0.0256% of LEZ's 33,554,432-cycle per-transaction budget. That share is computed from the constant the assertions use rather than from a rounded "32M", which is what an earlier draft did and why it said 0.027%. So P1's "single transaction" is comfortable rather than tight, and it is verification that decides whether a payload fits, which is what ADR 25 and ADR 26 already bound. The two figures are separate because `submit_price` has two paths: a first write builds the price account, an update decodes the published one first. The 1,196-cycle difference between them is a net between the two paths rather than a component -- an update pays for a read and for `publish`'s checks, a first write for a claim and for building and encoding the account -- and each of those four is measured on its own and pinned, without summing to the gap, because isolated calls do not cost what inlined ones do: the four-term estimate comes out at 655 against a gap of 1,196, about half way. The build figure is build and encode, observed through `core::hint::black_box` rather than a checksum, because a fold over the encoded bytes charged about 1,360 cycles of observation to the figure it was measuring. The recurring cost is the update's, since that is what every heartbeat runs. These are figures for the `submit_price` body: SPEL's generated validator derives the price account's address before the body is entered, which is 1,722 cycles measured separately, and the dispatcher and `SpelOutput` wrapping are outside every figure because reaching them needs the macro's entry point rather than a function call. That is the structure the requirement asks for, and it is not yet the evidence -- what a submission costs in cycles is M2-18, and the same update travelling through a real sequencer is M2-19. M3-06 is the pull side, and it has the same shape: `settle` reads the clock, verifies the payload it was handed and writes the order in one call, so acting on a price is one transaction. Not *no* prior transaction: a pull consumer establishes its authority and registers what it trusts for a feed before an order against that feed can settle. What it registers nothing with is the aggregator, which is F9's property rather than this one's; the single-transaction claim P1 is about is the settlement itself. `the_post_states_pass_lez` hands the result to LEZ's own `validate_execution` rather than restating its rules. What a pull read costs is M3-08, and it is this row's pull-side budget evidence rather than only P2's: the read is 3,041,427 cycles and the whole `settle` body 3,048,702, which are 9.06% and 9.09% of the 33,554,432-cycle budget, so a pull settlement fits with an order of magnitude to spare. Push mode's read is 6,803, 0.0203%. Both are asserted against the same constant the assertions divide by rather than a rounded budget. What is still missing is not structure and no longer the body's price: it is the term outside the body, because LEZ charges about 113 cycles a byte for instruction data before either program is entered and on the pull side that data is the payload. M3-10's byte accounting is what turns "the body fits" into "the transaction fits" for a payload of a given size, and ADR 26's `MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES` is what bounds the worst case in the meantime. Partial until M3-10 lands.

**P2** — Cost measurement as a primary deliverable: per-signer recovery, keccak256, decode, membership check and (push) account write and registration, per mode, reproducible from the test suite

"Reproducible from the test suite" is satisfied the strict way: every published figure is asserted by exact equality and runs in CI on x86_64. M0 measured the two primitives in isolation, and its per-component split comes from a subtraction rather than a residual: `lez_plumbing` is a third guest identical to `lez_verify` with the cryptography removed, so the framework's per-package instruction handling is taken out directly and `instruction_handling_cost_is_unchanged` pins it. Without that separation, drift in the framework's cost is silently reattributed to recovery. M1-25 does the same for the shipped path: `COSTS.md` breaks a real update into decode, keccak256, recovery, the signer-set check and a named remainder, by differencing prefixes of `verify_feed` in the product guest over payloads RedStone published. Recovery is 95.85% of a three-signer update and nothing amortises, so a wider threshold is linearly priced. The table is printed by the code that asserts it, so a published figure and an asserted figure cannot drift apart, and the two rows for keccak256 and recovery are what finally give ADR 6 its CI guards in cycles alone. The cross-architecture finding (M0-11) stands in the report, measured across three machines; ARM64 is not a delivery target and is no longer re-checked on every push. M2-18 closes the push write the same way, and with the same discipline: `submit_cost.rs` brackets the `submit_price` body rather than the pipeline -- the generated validator that derives the price account address before the body runs is measured separately, at 1,722 cycles, and the dispatcher and `SpelOutput` wrapping are outside every figure, each of its two cases is measured against its own stage 0 -- because the price account is built in setup, and subtracting across cases credited the update with 15,410 cycles it never paid, which is how the first version of this measurement was wrong -- and stage 2 has to report three post-states, so a submission that refused cannot publish as an implausibly cheap write. The two guests corroborate: they agree on verification to 42 cycles in 3,039,790, 0.0014%, which is the one figure here bounded rather than pinned exactly, because a cycle count is a property of a guest ELF and not of the work. Registration is the requirement's other push clause -- P2 asks for "(push) account write **and** registration" -- and it is measured too, in a guest of its own so that a stage added to the write's guest does not move it: a first registration is 5,270 cycles, 0.0157% of the per-transaction budget, cheap for the same reason the write is, which is that neither does any cryptography. The figure includes the `admin::authorise` gate the generated handler runs before delegating; without it the measurement was 3,821, which was the helper's cost and not a registration's. Measured on a first registration only; a re-registration after a deregistration takes a different branch and never runs on an operating path. M3-08 is the other side of the requirement's "per mode", and the figure a consumer author actually asks for: what obtaining a price costs. A pull read is 3,041,427 cycles and a push read is 6,803, a factor of 447, and the difference is not a tuning margin -- a pull consumer has nothing published to fetch, so its read *is* a verification and it pays that every time, while a push consumer decodes six fields somebody else verified once. 96% of the gap is signature recovery, asserted rather than claimed, and the remaining 4% is the rest of verification rather than something unaccounted for. What push mode avoids is recovery and not cryptography: `read_price` checks the account's address first, which derives two PDAs at 3,654 cycles, 54% of the whole read and its largest single item -- an earlier draft of `COSTS.md` said this mode hashed nothing, and it is now a measured stage rather than a remainder attributed to "the checks". Two figures per mode rather than one, because the only programs that perform a read are the reference consumers and each holds a limit order that is M3-05 and M3-06's domain rather than the mode's -- so the mode's read is published and the whole `settle` body beside it, at 3,048,702 and 13,282, and the small residual between them is itself the evidence that the domain is not where a read's cost goes. That residual is only comparable across modes because both stage 1s contain the same kind of work: the registration's decode on both sides and the order's on the pull side happen in the setup that cancels, after a first draft charged one mode's limit order to its read and the other's to its residual. `[M3-08:01]` records that choice and one thing found by measuring rather than by reasoning: adding two dependency edges to the pull consumer's guest manifest, for a binary that ships nowhere, moved `PULL_CONSUMER_ID` -- which is a program id and therefore every account the program owns -- so the crates re-export what their guests need instead and all three image ids were re-measured identical. The published account's decode first read 45 cycles for 136 bytes, which the component table prices at 1,442: an observation that returned one field let the optimiser elide the rest. The whole-`settle` stages had the same hole and hid it better, reporting only how many post-states came back, so every field of every returned account was a value nothing read -- a plausible figure rather than an implausible one, in the stage that dominates the table. `black_box` is the fix in both, for the third time in this file. What LEZ spends reading instruction data is outside every figure and falls asymmetrically -- a pull settlement carries the payload at about 113 cycles a byte, a push settlement a feed id -- which ADR 26 bounds and `COSTS.md` names, because a per-read comparison that omitted it would understate the pull side. Still to come is the byte accounting (M3-10).

**P3** — Documented cost delta between the in-program path and a hypothetical native ECDSA and keccak256 precompile, reported separately per mode

M0 delivered the first delta sketch against per-chain reference points. M3-09 splits it per mode, which is the form the requirement asks for, because a per-read pull path and a per-update push path amortise a precompile differently.

**S2** — End-to-end integration tests run against a standalone LEZ sequencer in CI, and CI is green on the default branch

The harness was standing from M1: CI boots a Bedrock node and a sequencer built from the same LEZ revision `lee_core` resolves to, and asserts it serves. M2-19 put adaptor traffic across it. `the_push_path_verifies_and_publishes_across_a_real_sequencer` deploys the guest, claims and initialises the admin, then for each of F7's five feeds registers it and submits a payload it signs for the chain's current round, reading each price account back -- and then does it again on BTC at a later round with a different value. Every assertion is on account state read from the chain and none is on what `sendTransaction` returned, because that call answers `Ok` for a transaction that was accepted and never executed: the reason appears only in the sequencer's log, so a test asserting the send is inert. Three things the host suite structurally cannot reach were found this way and are recorded in `[M2-19:01]` and the test's own comments: that accepted-is-not-executed distinction, that nonces are one per signer rather than one per account, and that `AdminUnowned` fires for real on a fresh chain exactly as `[M2-06:01]` predicts. The test resolves in its own workspace (`e2e/`) because reaching a sequencer over its typed RPC pulls the whole Bedrock node -- 384 packages to 798 in the product lockfile, and seven git sources the licence gate does not allow the product; `[M2-19:01]` records that decision and what it costs. M3-07 has since put the pull side's traffic across the same harness, in a second suite sharing the first's transport through `e2e/tests/support/chain.rs` rather than copying it -- included by path from each suite rather than declared in `e2e/src/lib.rs`, because a library edge is what put the Bedrock graph in front of the licence gate. The row stays partial for M1-03 alone: the workflow has to be green on the *default* branch, and both milestones are still integration branches.

**S3** — At least one test per hard requirement, including per mode: valid-signature acceptance, invalid-signature rejection, threshold boundaries, staleness, asset mismatch, invalid value, and (push) registration and signer-set transitions

This matrix is the requirement's own instrument. It is `partial` by construction until M5-06 leaves every row verified; the checker is what stops that from being asserted without evidence. S3 asks for valid-signature acceptance and invalid-signature rejection specifically: M1-21 verifies RedStone's published signatures over their published packages, while ADR 15 adds a payload with an unrecoverable signature alongside an otherwise valid quorum and requires `InvalidSignature`. M1-24 adds the coverage an example cannot give: the threshold, the framing and the scale conversion are claims about every input, and `verifier-core/src/properties.rs` generates them (ADR 21). The last of those tests is the one that matters most for a guest, since ADR 4 makes a panic on a malformed payload an aborted transaction rather than a rejection. M2-13 and M2-15 add the push mode's own half of the dimensions S3 names, which the M1 tests cover only in `verifier-core`: the freshness window from both sides rather than one (ADR 18 makes it two-sided, and the lower edge is what a chain clock that has fallen behind would meet), an unrecoverable signature over a payload RedStone really signed, and the threshold as a boundary -- three of five packages against a threshold of three and then of four, which is the only way to reach `ThresholdNotMet` here, since a partially-overlapping roster aborts on the first unknown signer instead (ADR 15). `ScalingOutOfRange` is not reachable from these captures, and `no_registrable_scale_lets_a_captured_price_overflow_its_conversion` records that rather than leaving a gap -- not that the push path cannot reach it, which a crafted correctly-signed value could. The signed values in the captures are fixed, so the feed's `decimals` is the only free parameter; it appears in a divisor, so `decimals = 0` is the most hostile registrable scale and the largest captured value, 6,281,896,137,270, is still seven orders of magnitude below what `u128` would refuse. The cause itself is `verifier-core`'s, over synthesised values. S3's "invalid value" is the other cause and M2-16 closes it: `ValueOutOfRange` is raised for a package carrying a zero, negative or over-wide value, before any scaling happens. No payload committed here can reach it -- the production captures contain no unusable value, which is the narrow claim rather than one about what RedStone will ever sign -- so `a_package_carrying_an_unusable_value_is_refused_by_the_submission_path` signs its own, over keys the feed is registered against, and drives both a zero and a negative through `submit_price`. Negative means the top bit of the full 32-byte value, which is what writing the test established: four bytes of `0xFF` right-align into a large positive number and publish. The builder is `verifier-core`'s own, reached through the `test-fixtures` feature rather than reimplemented, because a second encoder for one wire format is how two of them start disagreeing (`[M2-16:01]`). M2-15's other half, the signer-set update delay, is operational rather than a code path: `MANIPULATION-ANALYSIS.md` analyses it under "Signer-set update delays", so what it owes is that pointer and not another test.

A deliverable in its own right, and a prerequisite for U2 rather than a by-product of it.

## Adaptor Security

**SEC1** — Reject any package whose signer is not in the authorised signer set for the requested feed, in both modes

Both modes share one membership check in `verifier-core`. Every package carrying the requested feed is recovered and its signer must be in the configured set; the first unknown signer returns `UnauthorisedSigner` even when authorised packages already meet quorum. Packages for other feeds remain irrelevant and are skipped before recovery. ADR 15 records why this follows SEC1's literal contract and why a malicious submitter causing its own transaction to fail is not a feed-wide denial of service. Pull integration evidence is now here (M3-03): a payload whose packages for the requested feed carry a signer outside the consumer's roster is refused through `verify_price`, and a roster narrower than the payload refuses rather than verifying against the subset. That is the reading of ADR 15 a consumer has to plan around and `[M3-01:01]` records what it obliges; it is the same membership check the test beside it exercises, stated with the subset deliberate, and not additional coverage. The scope stays the requested feed throughout: a stranger reporting only another feed in the same payload is skipped before recovery and is not a refusal, which is SEC1's own wording and is pinned by `strangers_reporting_only_another_feed_do_not_report_unauthorised_signer`. Push integration evidence is M2-13: `a_signer_outside_the_registered_set_cannot_publish` drives a captured payload through `submit_price` against a feed registered with a roster that excludes one of its signers, so the refusal is the stored set's and not a unit test's fixture. Both halves are here.

**SEC2** — In push mode the stored signer set is updatable only by the admin authority, and the update path is tested; in pull mode the set comes from the consumer and never from the payload

Two obligations, and both have landed in part. Push: M2-08 replaces a feed's signer set and threshold together, behind the M2-06 gate, and the update path is tested rather than asserted -- the unit tests cover what a rotation decides, `tests/update_signer_set.rs` runs one against a feed `register_feed` really created and hands the post-states to LEZ, and three guest tests cover the generated validator. The set and the threshold move as one because a threshold is only meaningful against the set it counts, so shrinking a set below its threshold is one refusal rather than a window. A rotation also names its feed as well as addressing it (ADR 33), so an operator rotating five feeds cannot move the wrong one. M2-14 asserts the admin-only property end to end rather than per function, and it has to live in the guest suite: the gate is a Rust call inside the handler rather than a constraint the dispatcher applies, so a handler that dropped it would pass every host test and every generated-validator test. `only_the_stored_authority_can_rotate_a_signer_set` calls the handler twice over one config account -- a stranger is refused with the gate's own code, and the authority gets past it and is stopped by the next check instead, so what differs between the two calls is the signer and the gate is what noticed. Pull, library side: `pull-lib` never derives or extends the authorised roster from the payload. Verification does read signers out of the payload -- recovering one from each package that carries the requested feed is the whole mechanism, and packages carrying only other feeds are skipped before that cost -- but a recovered address is only ever a lookup key: it is accepted when it already appears in the separately supplied roster and is otherwise the refusal, and it never joins the roster or the set of addresses a later package is checked against. `verify_price` takes the roster and the payload as separate arguments, and the roster as a shared borrow, so nothing in the call can grow it. What M3-03 adds is naming and the configuration surface, not new verification coverage. `a_roster_narrower_than_the_payload_refuses_rather_than_narrowing` states the operational reading -- the set being the consumer's does not make it a dial, and `[M3-01:01]` records what that obliges an operator to coordinate -- but it is the membership check the test beside it already exercised. The threshold behaviour a wide roster turns on is `verifier-core`'s and is tested there once for both modes, which is what ADR 23 and F9's row say and what this row is not going to contradict. Neither are the roster guards: `FeedConfig::try_new` is `verifier-core`'s, `a_repeated_signer_is_rejected` and `more_signers_than_the_buffers_hold_is_rejected` assert both there, and the push path reaches the same function through `FeedAccount::config`. Being a pull consumer's only entry point to the signer set does not make the behaviour this crate's. What is this crate's is narrower and real: `a_roster_a_consumer_cannot_use_is_refused_when_it_builds_one` exercises those guards through `pull-lib`'s own re-exports, so dropping `ConfigError` or `MAX_SIGNERS` from them stops that file compiling. Nothing else in the suite names either, and CI runs no rustdoc, so the intra-doc links that mention them fail no build. Pull, consumer side: a shared borrow proves immutability during the call and says nothing about where the consumer got the roster. A consumer that copied it out of its own instruction data would satisfy every signature in `pull-lib` and defeat the requirement, so the boundary that had to be shown is a roster the caller cannot reach. M3-06 shows it, and shows it the way the push side does: what this consumer trusts for a feed -- its data service, its pair, its scale, its window, its roster and its threshold -- lives in a `FeedTrust` account the program owns, one per feed, written only behind an authority gate. `settle` takes an order account, a trust account, the clock and a payload; it writes neither of the two it reads for configuration, and there is no signer, threshold, window or pair parameter for instruction data to occupy. `nothing_in_settles_instruction_data_can_reach_the_signer_set` asserts that against the published IDL rather than against the source, because the IDL is what a caller builds against and an added parameter fails there rather than passing as a diff nobody read. What protects the roster is then the gate, asserted from both sides: `every_instruction_that_moves_what_the_program_trusts_declares_a_signer` over the IDL, the same name over SPEL's generated validators in the guest, and `only_the_authority_can_register_a_feeds_trust` and `only_the_authority_can_rotate` over the logic. The authority itself comes from a build input rather than from whoever arrives first -- `anybody_but_the_genesis_key_is_refused` -- and hands over in two steps, so a mistyped key costs a nomination rather than the program: `a_handover_takes_two_transactions_and_two_signers`. All of that is per feed, which is ADR 30's decision reaching its pull caller: a global roster cannot represent an estate where one feed's set has moved, and a threshold is only meaningful against the set it counts, so `FeedTrust` is the counterpart of the `FeedAccount` the push side stores rather than a second shape. Counterpart and not a copy: it carries the `dataServiceId` RFP-020 names in a pull consumer's configuration, and it has no pause flag, because pausing is an aggregator's lever over the feed it publishes and a consumer that wanted to stop acting stops sending settlements. A rotation moves the set and the threshold together and nothing else -- `a_rotation_replaces_the_set_and_the_threshold_together`, `a_rotation_changes_nothing_else_about_a_feed` -- names its feed as well as addressing it (ADR 33), and is refused before the write if the result would leave the feed unverifiable, so the old set is still in place when it fails. Every instruction that writes a feed's trust holds to ADR 33 that way, and a registration has to reach it differently: it may be handed a retired account, which is empty and remembers no feed id, so it compares the account's address against the one the named feed derives. `a_registration_cannot_be_written_into_another_feeds_account` is what pins that, and it is not decoration -- without the comparison a registration could write one feed's configuration into another's account, leaving the second answering `AlreadyRegistered` to a registration and `FeedMismatch` to a retirement, which are the only two ways out. `a_rotation_changes_which_payloads_verify_without_a_redeployment` is the one that makes the whole arrangement more than plumbing: over the captured signatures, narrowing the roster below the set that signed a payload refuses that payload and widening it invalidates nothing. `[M3-06:02]` records the rejected alternative and it is the instructive one: a compiled roster reads as the stricter choice and is worse than unnecessary. F9 asks for a configured tuple with no dependency on the aggregator's price account, not for a consumer that holds no state, so governed state satisfies it -- and since RedStone rotates on a multi-year schedule, a compiled roster would have met that certain event with a redeployment, which in LEZ moves every derived address and abandons every open order. Both halves are here.

**SEC3** — Minimum recommended `maxAge` documented for both modes, with a manipulation analysis covering signer compromise, replay of stale packages and signer-set update delays

M2-17 delivered the document, `MANIPULATION-ANALYSIS.md`: the `maxAge` recommendation and the analysis of signer compromise, replay and signer-set update delays. The window it reasons over is bounded at both ends now. `MAX_MAX_AGE_MS` is fifteen minutes, the default RedStone's own validator falls back to, so no feed may be looser than the upstream fallback. It is enforced rather than published because a `maxAge` past it degrades the check smoothly and never visibly breaks: at a year the window admits every real package without saturating at all, and only at the extreme does `freshness` saturate outright (ADR 29). Replay splits three ways and the document says so: a package replayed into a payload built around another moment refuses that payload (ADR 27), a replay whose packages fall outside the window is `StalePackage`, and an intact in-window round verifies -- its packages agree about the moment and its signatures are genuine, so what bounds it is `maxAge` together with the aggregator refusing a timestamp no newer than the stored one. `a_replayed_payload_is_refused_however_well_signed_it_is` covers the out-of-window case only, and its first assertion is the intact payload verifying. In push mode staleness cannot be defeated: `submit_price` reads the clock from an account the dispatcher hands it, so its id and its data are fields of one chain-supplied struct and no caller may substitute another. Pull mode is weaker and M3-01 records why -- a `no_std` library cannot take that struct, so `verify_price` receives an id and sixteen bytes as separate arguments and cannot tell that they came from the same account. What it does refuse is any account but the pinned one, which is the likely mistake given that the 10- and 50-block accounts hold plausible timestamps; binding the two is the consumer boundary's, and M3-06 is where it is exercised. In both modes a clock that cannot be read refuses rather than guesses, since verifying without one accepts a package of any age. The row stays partial for one reason: the recommended floor is provisional, because only one of its three terms has a measurement. M2-00 supplied that one and `FEEDS.md` records it -- rounds land every 10,000 ms and the worst gap observed was 20,000 ms, which is a lower bound on the worst gap rather than a ceiling, because a longer sample finds a longer one. The other two are open: a relayer has to exist before submission latency can be timed, and the skew between a signer's clock and the sequencer's is unmeasured and unbounded -- RedStone's three-minute forward tolerance is their default for the other side of the window, not a limit on a signer. Against a 120,000 ms floor the measured term spends 20,000, so the two unmeasured ones share about 100 seconds. The analysis also corrects the reading of the threshold that F3's wording invites: the price is a median, so two compromised keys control a 3-of-N feed rather than three. Four tests hold that arithmetic, one per row of the document's table, including the one showing a threshold of four is no harder to move than three, because an even count averages the middle two, and the one showing seven needs four, so the ratio does not improve as the threshold grows. Pull's weaker position is stated in the document plainly: a pull consumer keeps its own signer set fresh, because it bypasses the centrally administered one. What that does not mean is that no administrative transaction can reach a pull roster at all. The aggregator's cannot; the consumer's own can, and the reference consumer has one -- `trust::rotate_signers` behind its own authority. So the operational burden is not that a pull consumer has no rotation path but that it has its own, on its own schedule, and nobody else's rotation reaches it. M3-06 is where that is built and `[M3-06:02]` is where the reason it is state rather than a constant is recorded.

**OS1** — The deliverable is open source under a permissive licence, dual MIT and Apache-2.0, with no copyleft or BUSL dependency, transitive ones included

The dual licence and the mechanical gate are done: `cargo deny check licenses` runs on every pull request over the whole graph, transitive dependencies included, and BUSL-1.1 is denied outright, which is also what enforces the RedStone boundary. What is not done is the requirement's second half. It asks for **no copyleft dependency, transitive ones included**, and the gate currently passes because copyleft is admitted by named exception rather than absent. Nothing copyleft is linked into a shipped artefact, which is the reassuring half and worth stating precisely rather than generously: the LGPL-3.0 family (`malachite` and its four siblings, plus `downloader`) appears in `m0/Cargo.lock` only, reached through risc0 proving, and is absent from the product lockfile entirely; `option-ext` is MPL-2.0 and reaches the product graph as a *build* dependency only, through `risc0-build` -> `dirs` -> `dirs-sys`, so it runs during a build and links into nothing. What remains is that the exceptions exist, so passing CI proves the gate is enforced rather than that the requirement is met, and a `verified` row would claim the latter on the strength of the former. It stays `partial` until Logos rules on whether build-time and measurement-only copyleft satisfies the requirement's *transitive ones included*. See *Open: the LGPL-3.0 dependency in LEZ's host graph* in `m0/versions.md`. One part of the gate that was prose is now a test. `deny.toml` is one file for every workspace, so the seven git sources the end-to-end harness needs (`[M2-19:01]`) are permitted repository-wide, and the reason that was safe -- the product resolves none of them -- was an argument rather than a check. Each now carries a `# harness-only` marker and `traceability/tests/source_boundary.rs` asserts both directions: no marked source appears in any lockfile for something delivered, and every marked source appears in the harness's, so an allowance the harness has stopped using cannot sit there for the next dependency to inherit. "Delivered" is every committed lockfile but `e2e/`'s, which matters because `methods/guest/Cargo.lock` resolves separately and is what the guest ELF is built from -- a source reaching only the guest would ship while a root-only check called it absent. All three properties were checked by making them fail: a marked source in the root, one in the guest's lockfile, and a scan that finds neither. What is still prose is the LGPL claim above -- that the family is absent from the product lockfile holds today and nothing enforces it.
